results.result: Multicolour light sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) was adapted to provide unprecedented 3D resolution of tsetse fly tissue topology and enabled the first 3D analysis of trypanosome infection in the fly. The technique simultaneously visualized epithelial tissues, the peritrophic matrix, and individual trypanosomes with single-cell resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C32-C34, C118, C119, and C122 are strongly supported by the LSFM data presented in Figures 1-4 and Videos 1-4. The manuscript demonstrates high-resolution 3D reconstructions of intact tsetse tissues with multicolour labeling, showing individual parasites within complex tissue architectures. The novelty claim of 'first 3D analysis' is supported by the absence of prior comparable work cited.

results.result: LSFM revealed that the peritrophic matrix exhibits extreme convolution with extensive folding, producing channels, folds and crevices that increase surface area. The diameter and surface area increase significantly toward the posterior midgut, contradicting simplified representations in prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 and C119-C121 are well-supported by the 3D reconstructions in Figure 2 and Video 2, which clearly show the complex folded topology of the peritrophic matrix. The comparison with historical work (C120) and criticism of subsequent literature (C121) provides appropriate context for the significance of these findings.

results.result: Spatiotemporal mapping of trypanosome infection shows characteristic establishment in the posterior midgut (days 1-3), population decline (days 4-6), and invasion of the anterior midgut and proventriculus from day 7 onward, corresponding to crossing of the peritrophic matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by the heat map in Figure 3A and the 3D LSFM reconstructions in Figure 3C-D showing parasites in endoperitrophic (early) versus ectoperitrophic (late) spaces. The temporal progression is documented across 196 infected flies with appropriate sample sizes for each time point.

results.result: Comprehensive 3D morphometric analysis of eight developmental stages revealed stage-specific cell body shapes and flagellar attachment conformations. Key findings include: procyclic cells with 180° flagellar turns, mesocyclic cells lacking free flagellar tips with straight trajectories, epimastigotes with nearly free flagella achieving speeds >100 μm/s, and asymmetric division producing highly motile and nearly immotile daughter cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C76 are comprehensively supported by the 3D morphometric data in Figure 5 and Videos 5. The analysis includes fixed, fluorescently labeled cells from multiple flies with clear documentation of morphological features. The absence of undulating membranes (C50) and the detailed characterization of each stage provide a complete morphological atlas. The claim about asymmetric division (C70) producing vastly different motility is particularly well-demonstrated.

results.result: Dynamic cellular waveform analysis revealed stage-specific flagellar beating patterns and swimming speeds. Long procyclic cells reach >2× the speed of procyclic forms, mesocyclic cells show reduced amplitude waves with straight trajectories, mesocyclic-to-epimastigote transitions double beat frequency reaching >100 μm/s, while short epimastigotes achieve <10 μm/s due to lack of traveling waves.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58, C60-C61, C64-C66, C69, C75-C76 are supported by the waveform analysis in Figure 6 and Video 6, which shows frame-by-frame analysis of swimming cells with quantified speeds and frequencies. The 3D visualization of cellular waveforms over time provides clear evidence for the stage-specific differences in motility. However, the manuscript notes these are exemplary analyses rather than comprehensive statistics.

results.result: Solitary trypanosome swimming behavior is strongly influenced by microenvironmental factors, particularly confinement and boundary layers. Procyclic cells swim at ~69 μm/s with 25 Hz beat frequency in open spaces but reverse flagellar beats when mechanically hindered. Near-wall motion is a prominent feature of mesocyclic microswimmers.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C82-C83, C85, C90-C91 are supported by high-speed microscopy data in Figure 7 and Video 7, showing trypanosomes in various tissue compartments. The quantitative measurements of speed and frequency (C82) and observations of reversal behavior (C83) are clearly documented. The conclusion about environmental influence (C90) is well-supported by the range of behaviors observed across different confinement states.

results.result: Trypanosomes exhibit highly coordinated collective motion behaviors across a range of cell densities and confinement states. Groups frequently synchronize flagellar beats, can join or leave clusters by reversing beats, and at high densities produce superordinate wave patterns capable of moving tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by high-speed microscopy in Figure 8 and Video 8, showing various collective behaviors from small synchronized groups to large dense swarms. The observation that collective motion can move tissue (C96) provides evidence for significant force generation. The range of behaviors across different densities and developmental stages is well-documented.

results.result: High-speed fluorescence microscopy with nuclear and flagellar markers enabled quantitative single-cell tracking within swarms and identification of developmental stages. Persistently swimming cells in tissues averaged 15-25 μm/s (up to 40 μm/s in fluid spaces), and individual cells were tracked joining clusters, synchronizing, and leaving again, indicating hydrodynamic self-organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C100-C102 are supported by the tracking analysis in Figure 9 and Video 9, which shows color-coded speed tracks of individual cells in complex tissue environments. The ability to distinguish developmental stages by nuclear morphology (C97) and track individual cell behavior within swarms (C101) demonstrates the power of the fluorescent reporter system. The inference of hydrodynamic self-organization (C102) is reasonable based on the observed behavior.

results.result: Spontaneous synchronization and desynchronization of large trypanosome populations occurs on timescales of seconds, significantly faster than known chemotactic responses. This demonstrates that collective behavior can be self-organized by hydrodynamic interactions without chemical signaling or physical attachment to tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 are supported by the time-lapse observations in Figure 10 and Video 10, showing transitions between chaotic and synchronized states within seconds. The comparison with chemotactic timescales (C112, citing Oberholzer et al., 2010) provides strong evidence that the observed switching is too fast for chemical signaling. The inference that hydrodynamic interactions drive the behavior (C111, C113) is well-reasoned, though alternative mechanisms cannot be completely ruled out.

results.result: Flagellar beat frequencies are relatively constant within each morphotype, suggesting cell morphology defines basic beating parameters, while environmental physical factors determine speed and direction. This is consistent with the geometric clutch hypothesis where flagellar attachment to the cell body provides mechanical resistance controlling waveform.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157, C159, and C161 are supported by the waveform analysis showing consistent frequencies within stages (Figure 6) and variable speeds depending on environment (Figures 7-9). The connection to the geometric clutch hypothesis (C159, C161) is appropriately cited and represents a reasonable mechanistic interpretation, though direct experimental validation of this mechanism is not provided in this study.

results.result: The experimentally measured morphology of the mesocyclic stage agrees with earlier in silico predictions, specifically that the helical flagellar course angle is shallower than in bloodstream or procyclic forms.
results.evaluation: Claim C152 is supported by comparison of the morphometric data in Figure 5C with predictions from Alizadehrad et al., 2015. The visual comparison between mesocyclic (5C) and procyclic/bloodstream forms (5A, 5I) confirms the shallower helix angle. This validates the predictive power of the computational model.

results.result: The tsetse-trypanosome system represents the first enclosed host-parasite system amenable to detailed analysis of diverse microswimmers in defined natural microenvironments, providing a tractable model that bridges in vivo and in vitro studies with the ability to isolate and study any developmental stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C30, C117, C141, C146-C148 are supported by the comprehensive demonstration of methods spanning LSFM, morphometry, and high-speed microscopy across all developmental stages and tissue compartments. The novelty claim (C26) is reasonable given the unique combination of accessibility, developmental diversity, and analytical tractability. The ability to isolate stages directly from flies (C148) is demonstrated throughout.

results.result: T. brucei undergoes a complex developmental cycle in the tsetse fly involving genetically fixed physiological and morphological changes as parasites traverse various organs. Motility is necessary for successful infection and transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C27-C29 are well-established facts about trypanosome biology, appropriately cited to previous literature (Ooi and Bastin, 2013; Rotureau and Van Den Abbeele, 2013; Rotureau et al., 2014; Dyer et al., 2013). These provide essential background context for the study and are not novel findings of this work.

results.result: Fluorescent protein-expressing pleomorphic AnTat1.1 cell lines complete development through all morphological stages including production of mammalian-infective metacyclic forms.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is supported by Figure 3-Videos 1 and 2 showing motile metacyclic cells with nuclear GFP and PFR-GFP markers. This validation is essential for confirming that the fluorescent markers do not disrupt the developmental cycle, though more extensive characterization of infection rates would strengthen this claim.

results.result: The spatial information from LSFM enables quantitative assessment of confinement states and mathematical analysis of the peritrophic matrix maze, forming a basis for numerical simulations. The morphometric and waveform data provide realistic assessment of cellular preconditions for motile behavior and enable development of quantitative mathematical models.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126, C142, C147, C149-C151 describe potential applications and future work rather than completed analyses. While the data quality appears sufficient for these applications (C124, C149 supported by presented data), the actual mathematical analyses, simulations, and complementary in vitro studies (C125-C126, C142, C147, C151) are proposed but not demonstrated. The predictive validation with one prior model (C152) supports feasibility but is insufficient to fully validate these broader claims.

results.result: The system enables future microfluidic studies to test hypotheses about hydrodynamically controlled behavior, analyze collective switching, compare flow regimes with in vivo measurements, and elucidate patho-functional relevance of motility. Collective microswimmers produce forces capable of moving tissues, raising questions about their influence on the microenvironment.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C172 primarily describe future research directions and potential applications. While the observation that collective motion can move tissue (C172, C96) is supported by Video 8, most claims are speculative about future experiments (C164-C169) or potential biological implications (C170-C171). These represent reasonable next steps but are not demonstrated results of the current work.
